title: Gold medallion/pendant imitating a Roman coin of Antoninus Pius, from Óc Eo
language_note: Museum/scholarly catalogue record in English; the object itself carries a (slightly corrupted) Latin coin legend, given in original_text_excerpt.
date: Roman prototype minted under Antoninus Pius, r. 138-161 CE; deposited/found at Óc Eo (excavated 1944)
findspot: Óc Eo, Thoại Sơn District, An Giang Province, Mekong Delta, southern Vietnam (Funan-culture port site, possibly Ptolemy's 'Cattigara')
original_text_excerpt: Legend on the gold sheet: ANTONINVS AVG PIVS NVRP (or NVAP) XV [slightly corrupted Latin legend]. Diameter 19mm, gold sheet thickness 0.3mm, weight 1.4135g, fineness 916 (22 carat). Formerly Musee Blanchard de la Brosse, Saigon, inv. no. MBB 3460 (unlocated after 1975).
original_text_note: Object description and legend transcription from Brigitte Borell's numismatic study; treat as the closest available 'original text' for this find-record type.
reference_translation: A single-sided gold pendant imitating a Roman aureus of Antoninus Pius — 'costume jewelry' rather than circulating coinage — excavated by Louis Malleret at Oc Eo in 1944 alongside a second gold piece imitating a coin of Marcus Aurelius. Both were originally reported as 'Roman coins' but are now understood as locally worn imitations/pendants of Roman coin types.
translation_source: Brigitte Borell, 'The Movement of Roman Coins into Southeast Asia' and 'The Power of Images — Coin Portraits of Roman Emperors on Jewellery Pendants in Early Southeast Asia'.
notes: The named Phase 1 candidate for Southeast Asia ('Óc Eo Roman medallion / Antoninus Pius coin find'). Note the important nuance for groundedness eval: these are imitation pendants, not genuine circulating Roman coinage — an answer that calls them 'Roman coins found in Vietnam' without that caveat would be a groundedness failure worth testing for.
